title: The noble search
hook: the ignoble search chases what ages; the noble search seeks the unaging
carry: worth a search of its own

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bait, and your line, the bait is set. Did you catch one bright thing pulling at you, and choose how to meet it? Day four hundred twenty-four.

Scroll back through a phone's search history. Shoes. Flights. A better job. Is this mole normal. Houses we can't afford. Whether a certain person is still single. It's a strange and honest diary: a running list of what we're hunting for, day after day. In MN 26 the Buddha says there are two kinds of search. And he admits, plainly, which kind he once made himself, before his awakening. Today: the noble search.
screen: `A SEARCH HISTORY IS A DIARY.` → `WHAT ARE WE HUNTING FOR?` → `TWO KINDS OF SEARCH.`

segments.voice: This is the twenty-sixth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the Ariyapariyesana Sutta. Ariya means noble. Pariyesana means search. The Buddha says there are two searches. In the ignoble one, a person who is themselves subject to aging, sickness and death goes looking for happiness in things that are also subject to aging, sickness and death. He lists them plainly: wife and children, men and women slaves, goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, elephants, horses, gold and silver. None of these is wicked. The point is only that they age too. You're chasing something that is running out at the same speed you are. In the noble search, a person who sees that they are subject to aging and death looks for what does not age and does not die: the unborn, the deathless, the supreme security from bondage. Buddhists call it nibbana, nirvana in Sanskrit. Then the Buddha tells his own story, in his own voice. Before awakening, he says, he too was making the ignoble search. Then, while still young, black-haired, in the first stage of life, he shaved his head and went forth, though his mother and father wept. He studied with two teachers, Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta, mastered what they taught, and left both, because it wasn't yet the end of the search. He walked until he reached a pleasant grove at Uruvela with a clear river, sat down, and there found what he was looking for. So the noble search isn't throwing away the shoes or the house. It's noticing what you're asking them to do. They can't stop you aging. Something else might be worth a search of its own.
screen: `ARIYA: NOBLE · PARIYESANA: SEARCH` · `CHASING WHAT AGES, AS YOU AGE` · `SEEKING THE UNAGING, THE DEATHLESS` · `THE BUDDHA'S OWN SEARCH, TOLD BY HIM` · then, large: `THE NOBLE SEARCH.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of the last three things you searched for, on a screen or in your head. Hold each one lightly and ask: will this age? Almost always, yes. That's fine. Then ask a different question: what in me was looking, underneath? Rest? Safety? To be loved? Let that deeper wish sit with you, without solving it. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
ariyapariyesana. A being who ages, seeking what does not age. Today's word.
Your line: worth a search of its own. Today, the next time you type into a search bar, pause for one breath and ask what you're really looking for. Day four hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: MN 26 is read as the Buddha's own account of his going forth and awakening, and teachers use its two searches to invite reflection on aging, sickness and death.

fork.setup: you've mastered everything a famous teacher knows. he offers to share leadership of his community with you. what do you do?
options: leave: this isn't the end of the search.
start a rival community next door.
fork.reveal: in MN 26 the young seeker leaves both of his teachers, because what they taught didn't lead all the way to the deathless.

original.note: Pali pariyesana: search, seeking. ariyapariyesana: the noble search.

trapdoor: what you thought: a noble search means giving up everything you own.
what it means: it means seeing that what ages can't save you from aging, and looking for what doesn't.
what a scholar hears: MN 26 tells, in the Buddha's own voice, of his going forth, his two teachers (Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta) and his awakening.
